**Short answer: this is not your body "adjusting," and you should not keep riding it out.** Worsening wheezing and chest tightness within minutes of using a rescue inhaler is a recognized, potentially dangerous reaction to the drug itself, and a home oxygen reading dipping to 91% puts you at the edge of what asthma guidelines classify as life-threatening territory. You need a same-day medical evaluation — and if breathing gets hard fast, that means the emergency department, not a phone call.

**Why "getting worse right after I use it" matters so much**

Every FDA-approved label for albuterol (the medicine in virtually all blue rescue inhalers) carries a boxed-level warning about **paradoxical bronchospasm** — the exact opposite of what the inhaler is supposed to do. The label language is blunt: it "can produce paradoxical bronchospasm that may be life threatening. If paradoxical bronchospasm occurs, [the inhaler] should be discontinued immediately and alternative therapy instituted" (DailyMed, Albuterol Sulfate HFA label: https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=7bb5b6dd-9105-4ee7-b205-ed79cf4b371b). The patient-facing section of the same label says: "If this happens, stop using [it] and call your healthcare provider or get emergency help right away."

Two details in your story fit this pattern closely:

- **Timing.** Paradoxical bronchospasm is worsening breathing *shortly after dosing* — which is what you're describing.
- **The new canister.** The FDA label specifically notes that with inhaled formulations, paradoxical bronchospasm "frequently occurs with the first use of a new canister." You switched to a new inhaler three weeks ago. That's a meaningful coincidence, not noise.

There's a second, less dramatic possibility the label also flags: "Need for more doses than usual may be a sign of deterioration of asthma and requires reevaluation of treatment." In other words, even if the inhaler isn't directly causing the reaction, your underlying asthma may be destabilizing and the new inhaler situation may be masking it. Either way, the answer is reevaluation, not waiting.

**About that 91% reading**

Your baseline of ~95% is normal-ish (FDA says 95–100% is typical for healthy people, though people with lung disease can run lower). A drop to 91% is a **4-point fall from your own baseline** and sits **1 point below the 92% threshold** that major asthma guidelines use to mark severe/life-threatening exacerbations. The Australian Asthma Handbook classifies room-air SpO2 <92% as life-threatening asthma and calls for emergency oxygen (https://www.asthmahandbook.org.au/acute-asthma/adults-and-adolescents/managing-acute-asthma-in-adults-and-adolescents-in-the-ed); UK teaching materials use the same <92% cutoff for the life-threatening category. One published review notes that "oxygen saturation <92% in room air can predict admission" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6676463/).

Two honest caveats on the number itself:

- **Home pulse oximeters are estimates, not measurements.** The FDA warns they have "limitations and a risk of inaccuracy" affected by poor circulation, cold hands, skin pigmentation, skin thickness, nail polish, and movement (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/products-and-medical-procedures/pulse-oximeters and https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/pulse-oximeter-basics). Many cheap units sold online are "general wellness" products the FDA has never reviewed for clinical decision-making.
- **But the direction of the error doesn't rescue you.** An inaccurate reading could mean your true saturation is fine — or worse than 91. The FDA's advice is to never rely on the number alone and to weigh it against symptoms. Your symptoms (worsening wheeze, chest tightness, gasping) are pointing the same direction as the number. When a rough measurement and your body agree, treat it as real.

**Go to the ER / call emergency services now if any of these happen:**

- Gasping, or struggling to speak a full sentence in one breath
- Lips, face, or fingernails looking bluish or gray
- Rescue inhaler not relieving symptoms, or needing it more and more often
- Chest pain, confusion, exhaustion, or feeling like you can't keep going
- SpO2 staying at or below ~92%, or continuing to fall

**What to do even if you stabilize tonight**

1. **Don't just silently stop the inhaler — but don't keep dosing through a bad reaction either.** The label says to discontinue immediately if paradoxical bronchospasm occurs, but "alternative therapy instituted" means a clinician substitutes something else; stopping with nothing in hand and uncontrolled asthma is its own risk. Call your prescriber today, describe the pattern (worse within minutes of use, three weeks, new canister), and ask what to use in the meantime.
2. **Bring the inhaler to the appointment.** Batch/lot issues, a defective canister, or an excipient you're reacting to are all things a clinician can check or document — and it matters for any report to the FDA's MedWatch program.
3. **Ask about a spacer**, even if your technique was signed off. A spacer reduces oropharyngeal deposition and cold-propellant "kick," which some people find triggers coughing or tightness.
4. **Get a written asthma action plan.** GINA (the global asthma guideline body) recommends every patient have one covering when to step up treatment, when to start oral steroids, and "how to get urgent medical care if symptoms continue or worsen" (GINA 2024 Summary Guide: https://ginasthma.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/GINA-Summary-Guide-2024-WEB-WMS.pdf).
5. **Mention how often you're using the blue inhaler.** GINA and the UK's MHRA both warn that SABA-only or SABA-heavy treatment is linked to more severe exacerbations and asthma deaths, and that anyone needing reliever more than twice a week needs their maintenance therapy reviewed (MHRA Drug Safety Update: https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/short-acting-beta-2-agonists-saba-salbutamol-and-terbutaline-reminder-of-the-risks-from-overuse-in-asthma-and-to-be-aware-of-changes-in-the-saba-prescribing-guidelines). Three weeks of escalating rescue use is exactly the signal that review is meant to catch.

**Uncertainty, stated plainly:** I can't diagnose you from here. It's possible this is paradoxical bronchospasm to the new inhaler, possible your asthma is deteriorating for an unrelated reason (new trigger, infection, expired or faulty canister), and possible your oximeter is simply unreliable. But none of those possibilities is "wait and see." The combination of *symptoms worsening right after dosing* plus *oxygen dipping below the guideline danger line* is a same-day medical problem, and potentially an emergency-department problem. Err on the side of going in.

# Research Report: Evert Calderon, Mesa Group Consulting, and the SuperMoney / Novae Partnerships

## Bottom line

Evert Calderon is using **SuperMoney as a monetization layer** and **Novae as a product fulfillment / revenue-share layer** for a new "marketplace" section of mesagroupconsulting.com. The Miro board you saw is a page-by-page roadmap for that section, and it maps almost exactly onto the live "Mesa Marketplace" navigation already on his site (Credit Cards, Personal Loans, Auto Loan Refi, Student Loan Refi, Debt Consolidation, Debt Relief, Trust & Will, Life Insurance) — https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/. His homepage states the relationship explicitly: *"Strategic Partnerships: We work with trusted names like SmartCredit, SuperMoney, and Novae, tools that already serve millions of people."*

The split on the Miro board follows a clear business logic:

- **SuperMoney pages** (credit cards, personal loans, auto refi, student loan refi, debt consolidation) are **commodity, self-serve lending products** that convert via pre-qualification forms and pay per lead/approval. SuperMoney provides the widgets, tracking links, and lender network; Evert provides the traffic and earns commissions.
- **Novae pages** (debt relief, trust & will, life insurance, business debt relief, business credit) are **higher-touch, higher-ticket, done-for-you services** that Novae fulfills (or routes to its own partners) and that pay much larger, often residual, commissions.

---

## 1. What SuperMoney is

SuperMoney (SuperMoney, LLC, Santa Ana, CA; founded June 18, 2013 by Miron Lulic) is a **financial comparison platform and personal finance app — not a lender, bank, or financial institution** (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuperMoney; https://help.supermoney.com/article/50-is-supermoney-a-lender; https://www.supermoney.com/is-supermoney-legit). It operates a marketplace spanning 50+ consumer finance categories (personal loans, credit cards, auto loans, student loans, banking, insurance, debt consolidation, etc.), where users compare offers, read reviews, and get pre-qualified offers via a single soft-pull form (https://www.supermoney.com/about; https://help.supermoney.com/article/61-what-does-supermoney-do).

**How SuperMoney itself makes money:** commissions from financial institutions when a user takes a product found through the platform, plus app subscriptions and advertising (https://help.supermoney.com/article/62-how-does-supermoney-make-money).

### The part that matters for Evert: SuperMoney's publisher/affiliate program

SuperMoney runs an explicit program for people exactly like Evert — site owners with an audience of credit-challenged consumers who want to monetize that traffic (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize):

- **"SuperMoney helps publishers monetize their traffic with tools for offering a wide range of financial products to their users. In addition to static offer links, your users can pre-qualify for personal loan offers from leading online lenders in real-time without having to leave your site. We keep your brand front-and-center."**
- **Super Links** — tracked referral links into 50+ finance verticals: *"Simply use a provided tracking link and start earning commission"* (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize/super-links).
- **Embeddable widgets / "Money Marketplace"** — personal loan pre-qualification, banking, and auto refinance widgets that run on the partner's own site (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize/money-marketplace).
- **White-label marketplaces** — *"Many lenders build out their own financial marketplaces entirely powered by SuperMoney's 50+ widgets to offer a variety of products, like deposit accounts, credit cards, tax relief, debt settlement, auto refi loans, and many more… you will never be charged a platform fee… SuperMoney actually pays its partners a rev-share of the commissions it receives"* (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize/prequalification-platform).

**Economics (public benchmark figures from affiliate networks):**

| Product | Published payout benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Credit cards | ~$50 commission per approval; CPA offers listed at ~$65; 60–75% rev-share variants | https://www.revshare.so/programs/advertiser/supermoney-credit-cards-0de12e53; https://www.affplus.com/o/supermoney-personal-credit-cards-revshare-us-6 |
| Personal loans | 75% rev-share CPA listings; "earn commissions **per qualified lead** instead of waiting for a funded loan"; "some of the highest EPCs in the space" | https://www.affplus.com/o/supermoney-cps-supermoney-personal-loans-desk-mob-us-75; https://www.flexoffers.com/affiliate-programs/supermoney-affiliate-program/ |
| General marketplace | Up to 30% per sale via Takeads | https://takeads.com/merchants/supermoney-us/ |

The underlying lender network spans prime to subprime (SoFi, LendingClub, Upgrade, Best Egg, Rocket Loans, OppLoans, NetCredit, Reprise, etc.), which matters for Evert's credit-repair clientele (https://www.supermoney.com/quotes/personal-loans/own-up?network=partner&offer_id=1191&aff_id=1145).

**What Evert is likely doing with SuperMoney, concretely:** the five "supermoney affiliate" pages on the Miro board are almost certainly (a) SEO/content pages on mesagroupconsulting.com with SuperMoney tracking links, and/or (b) pages embedding SuperMoney's pre-qualification widgets under Mesa's own branding. The credit cards page is already live and matches this pattern exactly: a card-matching flow ("Pre-qualified offers… Compare 400+ cards… Match based on your credit profile") with a "Powered by [logo]" attribution and the disclosure *"Mesa Group Consulting is not a card issuer. We help you compare offers from our partners and may earn a referral fee if you're approved, at no extra cost to you"* (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/credit-cards).

---

## 2. What Novae is

Novae (Novae, LLC, 1506 Klondike Road Ste 403, Conyers, GA; founded 2014) describes itself as *"a fintech company that provides greater access to credit, capital, and entrepreneurship for consumers and small businesses nationwide, with a particular interest in empowering underserved communities"* (https://novaemoney.com/; https://novaemoney.com/base/compensation-plan). It is a **member of the Direct Selling Association** — i.e., a direct-selling/MLM-style distribution model, not a conventional fintech (stated in the footer of Novae's product pages, e.g., https://novaemoney.com/life-insurance/).

Key point: **Novae is not a lender and does not perform credit repair for clients.** Its own loan page says: *"No, Novae is simply a site that allows prospective borrowers to apply to be pre-qualified or pre-approved for a loan through a network of lenders"* (https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/novae-money-loans), and its consumer disclaimer says: *"Novae provides self-directed credit software, credit education and credit monitoring tools. Novae does not work on your credit for you, and no score increase, item removal, approval, funding or timeline is promised… No income is guaranteed, and most participants should not expect substantial income"* (https://novaemoney.com/consumers/).

### Novae's product catalog (relevant to the Miro board)

- **Debt relief / "Debt Help"** — debt settlement/negotiation for unsecured debts (credit cards, collections, medical): requires **$10,000+ in debt**, claims reduction of monthly payments "up to 50%," resolution in "20–48 months," no upfront fees (performance-based per FTC rules) (https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/debt-help).
- **Business debt relief** — a parallel program for business debts (listed across Novae's site navs, e.g., https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/business-debt-help).
- **Business credit builder** — "$995 one-time" DIY or "$2,495" guided tier, promising positioning to "access at least $50,000 in credit lines" (explicitly *"not a loan or grant"*) (https://novaemoney.com/biznestfunding/business-credit).
- **Business funding** — a funding program offered "in ALL 50 STATES" (https://novaemoney.com/ericlh/business-funding-programs).
- **Life insurance** — explicitly fulfilled through a **Policygenius partnership**: *"we've partnered with Policygenius, a trusted leader in the industry… personalized quotes from top insurers"* (https://novaemoney.com/life-insurance/).
- **Trust & will plans** — "Start a Trust" / "Start a Will" pages (https://novaemoney.com/corporate/trusts; https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/wills); Mesa's own disclosure separately names **Trust & Will** (trustandwill.com) as the estate-planning platform (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure), suggesting Novae's trust funnel routes to a provider like Trust & Will.
- Plus myNovaeCredit monitoring, myNovaeDisputes (AI dispute letters), credit cards, auto/student refi, tax prep, LLC formation, etc. — the same categories as SuperMoney, but sold through Novae's funnel.

### Novae's affiliate/co-brand model (the part Evert is using)

- **Affiliate program:** *"Earn up to $3,000+ per referral depending on the program your customer enrolls for and potentially grow a residual income,"* with a replicated NovaeMoney.com site and marketing tools (https://novaemoney.com/become-an-affiliate/). Enrollment tiers carry their own costs — per Novae's affiliate enrollment agreement, roughly **$99 + $49/mo (Basic), $299 + $69/mo (Plus), $499 + $99/mo (Pro)**, with payouts of "up to $4,000/customer" on premium offerings (https://novaemoneytraining.com/wp-content/uploads/Affiliate_Enrollment_Agreement.pdf).
- **Debt-help commission math** (from Novae's compensation plan site): *"Affiliates earn 50% of the commission paid to Novae (typically 25% of the client's monthly budget payment)"*, plus 10% of recurring monthly fees paid to the partner — i.e., **residual income for the life of a 20–48-month debt settlement enrollment** (https://novaepays.com/sales-commissions/).
- **Co-Brand Program** — the most likely fit for what the Miro board shows: *"A Curated financial services turn-key web package, powered by Novae"* with **19 tailored sales pages and 20+ embedded forms/applications/lead magnets**, covering exactly the Novae-labeled items on Evert's board: Business Credit Builder, Business Funding, Business Debt Relief, Personal Loans, Debt Consolidation, Consumer Debt Relief, Instant Tax Refund, Student Loan & Auto Refi, Savings Accounts & Credit Cards (https://novaemoney.com/credithelp/cobrand-program). There's also a "Fintech Career Accelerator & Co-Brand Program" (12-month mentorship plus your own co-branded fintech platform) (https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/novae-money-loans, nav).

---

## 3. Who Evert is and how this fits Mesa Group Consulting

Evert Jafet Calderon is the founder/owner ("Visionary Operations Officer" per his LinkedIn) of **Mesa Group Consulting** (MESA & CO CONSULTING LLC), a credit repair and business funding company at 5001 California Ave Suite 219, Bakersfield, CA, founded 2023, claiming 2,500+ clients and a 5.0 Google rating, serving clients in English, Spanish, and Punjabi (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/; https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/author/evert-calderon; https://linkedin.com/in/evertcalderon; https://ccasite.org/members/score-certified/organization/Mesa+Group+Consulting/). Core offerings include Mesa360 full-service credit repair, a Creditily DIY platform, Mesa × SmartCredit monitoring subscriptions, Mesa Financial Concierge, and Mesa Group Capital for business funding (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/creditily; https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/concierge).

His site's own **Affiliate Disclosure** confirms all three legs of the structure you're asking about (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure):

- **SuperMoney** — "Financial product comparison platform offering personal loans, auto loan refinancing, student loan refinancing, debt consolidation loans, and credit card comparisons" — commission when users use referral links or secure products. (This is a verbatim match to the five "supermoney affiliate" items on the Miro board.)
- **Novae** — "Business funding and debt relief services (business and personal)," and "Novae and Partner Networks: Debt settlement and negotiation services" — commission on funding secured or debt-relief enrollments.
- **Trust & Will** and **PolicyGenius** — direct affiliates for estate planning and life insurance (the same fulfillers Novae itself uses).
- Plus SmartCredit, Ava Finance, CreditStrong, Self, rent-reporting services, and Experian Boost on the credit-building side.

His disclaimer adds: *"We may receive compensation through affiliate partnerships and referral arrangements. Credit repair services comply with CROA"* (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/).

---

## 4. Page-by-page reading of the Miro board

| Miro board item | Label | What Evert is almost certainly doing | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit cards | supermoney affiliate | SuperMoney-powered card-matching/pre-qualification page under Mesa's brand; ~$50/approval type commissions | Live page with "Powered by" matcher + referral-fee disclosure (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/credit-cards); SuperMoney cards affiliate ~$50 (https://www.revshare.so/programs/advertiser/supermoney-credit-cards-0de12e53) |
| Personal loans | supermoney affiliate | SuperMoney pre-qual widget or tracked link into its multi-lender offer engine; paid per qualified lead | SuperMoney publisher program language (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize); per-lead payouts (https://www.flexoffers.com/affiliate-programs/supermoney-affiliate-program/) |
| Auto loan refi | supermoney affiliate | SuperMoney auto-refinance widget ("average U.S. auto loan exceeding $25,000") | https://www.supermoney.com/monetize/money-marketplace |
| Student loan refi | supermoney affiliate | Same pattern into SuperMoney's student-loan refi vertical | https://www.supermoney.com/monetize (50+ verticals incl. student loans) |
| Debt consolidation loan | supermoney affiliate | Personal-loan-for-debt-consolidation flow via the same engine | SuperMoney lists debt consolidation among its categories (https://takeads.com/merchants/supermoney-us/) |
| Debt relief | novae | Novae's debt settlement program ($10k+ debt, 20–48 months); Mesa earns ~50% of Novae's commission (typically 25% of the client's monthly payment), residual | https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/debt-help; https://novaepays.com/sales-commissions/ |
| Trust & will plan | novae | Novae's trust/will funnel (which routes to an estate-planning provider; Mesa also holds a direct Trust & Will affiliate) | https://novaemoney.com/corporate/trusts; https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure |
| Life insurance | novae | Novae's Policygenius-powered life insurance quote funnel | https://novaemoney.com/life-insurance/ |
| Business debt relief | novae | Novae's business debt help program | https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/business-debt-help (nav) |
| Business credit | novae | Novae's business credit builder ($995/$2,495 programs, "$50K+" positioning) | https://novaemoney.com/biznestfunding/business-credit |

The clean division of labor: **SuperMoney = high-volume, self-serve, click-and-apply consumer credit products** where Mesa's role is traffic and a branded front end; **Novae = consultative, done-for-you, high-ticket programs** (debt settlement, business credit/funding) where a single enrollment can be worth up to ~$3,000+ and/or a monthly residual for years — a natural fit for a credit-repair firm whose clients graduate into debt cleanup and business funding.

---

## 5. Quantitative summary of the economics

- SuperMoney affiliate benchmarks: ~$50 per credit-card approval; personal-loan offers listed at 60–75% rev-share CPA; up to 30% per sale via Takeads; per-qualified-lead payment on loans (sources in table in §1).
- Novae: up to $3,000+/referral on premium programs; debt-help affiliates earn 50% of Novae's commission (typically 25% of the client's monthly budget payment) plus 10% of recurring partner fees; Novae affiliate enrollment itself costs ~$99–$499 upfront plus $49–$99/month depending on tier (https://novaemoney.com/become-an-affiliate/; https://novaepays.com/sales-commissions/; https://novaemoneytraining.com/wp-content/uploads/Affiliate_Enrollment_Agreement.pdf).
- Example of the residual logic: a client with $15,000 of credit-card debt enrolls in Novae's debt-help program (20–48-month timeline per https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/debt-help). If Novae's commission is ~25% of that client's monthly payment and Mesa receives 50% of Novae's commission, Mesa earns a cut of every monthly payment for potentially 2–4 years — versus a one-time ~$50–$75 on a credit-card approval from the SuperMoney side. That asymmetry explains why the "services" half of the board is labeled Novae.

---

## 6. Caveats and uncertainties

1. **The "Powered by" logos on Mesa's live pages did not render in my fetches**, so I could not visually confirm the SuperMoney widget on the credit-cards page; the attribution is based on the page's card-matching flow, Mesa's own affiliate disclosure naming SuperMoney for exactly those five categories, and the homepage naming SuperMoney as a strategic partner.
2. **"Trust & will plan — novae" is ambiguous**: Novae has its own trust/will pages, and Mesa separately discloses a direct Trust & Will affiliate relationship. The Miro label likely just means "fulfilled through the Novae package," with Trust & Will (or similar) as the ultimate provider. Same for life insurance, where Novae's fulfiller is Policygenius.
3. **Novae's own consumer-lending pages resemble a white-labeled offer engine** (one form, 30+ banks, loans $500–$100,000, APR from 5.99% — https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/novae-money-loans), which is structurally similar to SuperMoney's engine, but I found no public evidence naming the provider behind Novae's loan pages; I can't confirm whether Novae and SuperMoney interconnect.
4. **Exact commission rates between Mesa and each partner are confidential** — Mesa's disclosure explicitly says amounts are "confidential and subject to non-disclosure agreements" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure). All dollar figures above are public benchmarks, not Mesa's actual terms.
5. **Regulatory posture worth noting**: Novae is a DSA-member direct-selling company whose own disclaimers state no income is guaranteed and "most participants should not expect substantial income" for its affiliates (https://novaemoney.com/consumers/); its business-credit "$50K+" figure is explicitly "not a loan or grant" (https://novaemoney.com/biznestfunding/business-credit). Mesa's pages, by contrast, carry CROA-compliant credit-repair disclosures and no-guarantee language, which suggests awareness of the compliance exposure that comes with reselling these programs.

**In one sentence:** Evert is building an affiliate-monetized "Mesa Marketplace" on his credit-repair site — using SuperMoney's free publisher platform to monetize commodity lending traffic (cards and loans, paid per lead/approval), and using Novae's paid affiliate/co-brand ecosystem to fulfill and monetize high-ticket, residual-income services (debt settlement, business credit/funding, insurance, and estate planning) for the same credit-repair clientele.

# Maternal Health in Cox's Bazar (Rohingya) vs. Mae La (Karen) Refugee Settings, 2017–2023: Indicators, Delivery Models, and Funding Shocks

## 1. Scope, settings, and evidence base

**Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh.** Following the August 2017 influx, roughly 900,000–950,000 Rohingya refugees lived in 34 camps in Teknaf and Ukhia upazilas (945,953 camp residents including Bhasan Char as of mid-2022), with >60 births/day recorded across the camps (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12613593/; https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/external_sitrep_july_-sep_2022_unfpa_coxs_bazar_comms.pdf). Maternal health services are delivered through a parallel humanitarian system coordinated by the SRH Working Group (UNFPA-led) under the Health Sector, with facility-based surveillance through the Maternal and Perinatal Mortality Surveillance and Response (MPMSR) system (established 2019 after the 2018 Reproductive Age Mortality Study, RAMOS) (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2022.pdf.pdf).

**Mae La, Thailand.** Mae La is the largest of nine Thai-Myanmar border "temporary shelters" (population ~34,325 in early 2021; 37,786 in 2016; historically reported up to ~50,000), predominantly Karen (https://www.zhiyanbao.cn/index/partFile/5/unhcr/2022-03/5_17005.pdf; https://access.archive-ouverte.unige.ch/access/metadata/a48a190f-537b-4b32-b37d-9bf63d9e7c48/download; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3749980/). Obstetric care has been provided by the Shoklo Malaria Research Unit (SMRU) — sole ANC/delivery provider since 1997 — with general health services run successively by MSF (to 2005), AMI/PU-AMI (2005–2015+), and subsequently IRC- and Malteser International-supported facilities reporting into UNHCR's integrated Refugee Health Information System (iRHIS) (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0172007; https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/2024-06/Asia%20-%20Thailand%20MCO%20ARR%202023.pdf).

**Data availability caveats (stated up front).** (a) The UNHCR iRHIS site reports for 2021–2023 were not retrievable in this research (server returned unreadable content), so Mae La's most recent verifiable UNHCR indicator data here are the 2017–2018 site reports; 2021–2023 Thai-side claims rest on peer-reviewed studies and UNHCR narrative reports. (b) No source reports *incidence rates* of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) for either setting; only cause-of-death proportions and referral audit data exist. (c) Cox's Bazar neonatal mortality is reported as perinatal death counts (surveillance began August 2023), not a NNMR per 1,000. (d) The premise of a discrete "2021 UNFPA funding reduction" affecting *both* locations is only partially supported by the evidence — see Section 6.

## 2. Core indicator comparison

| Indicator | Cox's Bazar (Rohingya) | Mae La (Karen) |
|---|---|---|
| ANC 4+ visits | ~17% (2021/22 Health Bulletin); 47% accessed *no* ANC (April 2023 survey); mean 6.9 visits in 2023–24 research cohort | ~89–91% ANC coverage (UNHCR HIS 2017–18); >90% completing 4+ visits (2000–2018 camp study) |
| Skilled birth attendance / facility delivery | 22% (early 2018 est.) → 35% (Jun 2019) → 73% (Aug 2022) → 85% (2023, UNFPA) | 96% (2017), 95% (2018) SBA; 75% deliver at SMRU clinic |
| PPH | No incidence rate; hemorrhage = leading cause of maternal death (26.7%–48% of deaths, 2020–2024) | No incidence data; active management of third stage documented as routine good practice |
| Neonatal/perinatal mortality | 304 perinatal deaths Aug–Dec 2023; 491 in 2024 (~10/week); derived ≈33/1,000 total births (see calculation) | NNMR 8/1,000 (UNHCR 2017); historical decline 21.8 → 10.7/1,000 (2008–2011) |
| Maternal mortality | MMR 179/100,000 (95% CI 130–228, RAMOS 2017–18); 45–96 maternal deaths/yr 2020–2024 | 1 maternal death (2017), 0 (2018); MMR 126.5/100,000 in comparison border camps (2000–2018) |

### 2.1 Antenatal care (4+ visits)

**Mae La.** UNHCR HIS site reports show ANC coverage of 89% (2017) and 91% (2018) against a >90% standard (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/39ea9ee8-f0f1-3911-a9c5-b75ce55bc944/Thailand_2017_Maela.pdf; https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/TH/Thailand_2018_Maela.pdf). The 18-year retrospective analysis of border camps (Mae Ra Ma Luang and Mae La Oon — the closest peer-reviewed proxy for Mae La's camp system) found **more than 90% of pregnant women attended four or more ANC visits**, with essential ANC elements scoring >90% on record review in Mae La's SMRU clinic (supplements, risk-factor recording, partogram use) (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/primary-health-care-research-and-development/article/mother-child-and-adolescent-health-outcomes-in-two-longterm-refugee-camp-settings-at-the-thaimyanmar-border-20002018-a-retrospective-analysis/5A2A03E5B33226D61F84A028BB229992; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25652646/). Approximately 90% of Mae La's pregnant women attend SMRU ANC clinics (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3749980/).

**Cox's Bazar.** Coverage is dramatically lower and measurement-heterogeneous:
- The Health Bulletin (Aug 2022) and MSNA 2021 reported **only ~17% of pregnant women receiving 4 ANC visits** (https://projects.hpc.tools/project/196334/view).
- A large April 2023 cross-sectional survey found **~47% of women accessed no ANC at all** in their most recent pregnancy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10835278/).
- In contrast, the iRRRd birth cohort (2,322 women recruited 2023–24) recorded a mean of 6.9 visits (SD 2.6) with 80.5% first-trimester initiation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12781834/) — a discrepancy plausibly reflecting facility-linked recruitment (women already engaged with services) versus camp-wide household surveys.
- Among women who *died*, 51% had received ≥4 ANC visits in 2023 (reported as a decline from 42% in 2022 — the direction of this year-on-year comparison is inconsistent in the source text) and 78% in 2024 (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2024-09/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202023%20Final.docx.pdf; https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2025-08/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202024%20Final.docx.pdf).

**Comparison:** Mae La's 4+ ANC completion exceeds Cox's Bazar's camp-wide estimate by a factor of roughly 5 (≈90% vs ≈17%), a gap attributable to the Thai-side system's 35-year continuity, single accountable ANC provider, and short geographic distances, versus Cox's Bazar's fragmented ~200-facility NGO landscape.

### 2.2 Skilled birth attendance

**Mae La.** SBA was 96% of all births in 2017 and 95% in 2018 per UNHCR HIS (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/39ea9ee8-f0f1-3911-a9c5-b75ce55bc944/Thailand_2017_Maela.pdf; https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/TH/Thailand_2018_Maela.pdf). Note an internal tension in the data: 75% of Mae La women deliver *at the SMRU clinic* (https://access.archive-ouverte.unige.ch/access/metadata/a48a190f-537b-4b32-b37d-9bf63d9e7c48/download), so the ~95% SBA figure likely credits camp-based trained birth workers/SBA-supervised home births; the reader should treat the SBA and facility-delivery figures as distinct constructs. The two-camp (MRML/MLO) study found 80% SBA over 2000–2018 (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/primary-health-care-research-and-development/article/mother-child-and-adolescent-health-outcomes-in-two-longterm-refugee-camp-settings-at-the-thaimyanmar-border-20002018-a-retrospective-analysis/5A2A03E5B33226D61F84A028BB229992).

**Cox's Bazar.** Facility-based delivery (the operational proxy for SBA, since SBAs are facility-based) rose from ~22% of deliveries in early estimates and 35% by June 2019 (https://scienceportal.msf.org/api/assets/7744/download/13930?filename=Hadiuzzaman+et+al+2022+Why+mothers+give+birth+at+home+exploration+of+Rohingya+refugees%E2%80%99+perceptions%2C+experiences%2C+and+expectations+regarding+maternity+services+in+Cox%E2%80%99s+Bazar%2C+Bangladesh.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8195412/), to 47% in 2018 JRP reporting (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/referral_trasportation_study_report.pdf), **73% by August 2022** (https://projects.hpc.tools/project/196334/view), and **85% in 2023**, with facility deliveries doubling from 4,870 (2018) to 6,064 (2020) and >10,600 safe births facilitated by UNFPA partners in 2023 alone (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/funding-gap-increased-insecurity-jeopardize-lives-rohingya-women-and-girls; https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/4-years-rohingya-refugee-influx-unfpa-remains-committed-supporting-women-and-girls-coxs-bazar). MSF alone assisted 2,192 births in the first 17 months of the crisis (https://www.msf.org/we%E2%80%99ve-provided-one-million-consultations-cox%E2%80%99s-bazar-5-things-weve-found-bangladesh-rohingya).

**Comparison:** Mae La achieved >90% SBA *before* 2017 and sustained it; Cox's Bazar started ~22–35% post-influx and reached 73–85% only by 2022–2023 after intensive ambulance/shuttle and TBA-engagement investments. Even in 2023, home delivery remained the modal choice among women who died (67% of community maternal deaths delivered at home) (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2025-08/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202024%20Final.docx.pdf).

### 2.3 Postpartum hemorrhage

**No direct incidence rate exists for either setting** — this is a genuine evidence gap, not an oversight.

**Cox's Bazar proxies:**
- RAMOS (Sept 2017–Aug 2018): obstetric hemorrhage was the leading cause of pregnancy-related death at 28%; of hemorrhage deaths, **61% were PPH and 39% antepartum hemorrhage** (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/Final%20RAMOS%20Summary%20Report%20for%20circulation_0.pdf).
- MPMSR cause-of-death proportions: 26.7% of 45 maternal deaths (2020; 8 PPH, 4 APH) → 29.2% of 96 (2021) → **44% of 83 (2022)** → 35% of 57 (2023; n=20) → 48% of 46 (2024) (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/annual_report_of_mpmsr_2020_03_august_2021.pdf; https://reliefweb.int/report/bangladesh/maternal-and-perinatal-mortality-surveillance-and-response-mpmsr-rohingya-refugees-response-coxs-bazar-bangladesh-annual-report-2021; https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2022.pdf.pdf; https://journals.diu.edu.bd/index.php/jegh/article/download/102/23/557).
- Facility audit 2020: obstetric hemorrhage caused 10 of 24 facility maternal deaths. A 2022 midwife-led birthing centre audit: of 43 women with significant complications among 337 booked, 10 (23%) were referred for PPH (https://exa.ai/library/publication/7cq1zmlq654).
- UNFPA's August 2021 report noted most facility maternal deaths "resulted as consequences of home trial followed by prolonged labour," with women arriving with retained placenta and PPH (https://www.bmj.com/content/375/bmj.n2722). Chronic anemia and hypertensive disorders — both PPH risk factors — are widespread in the camps (https://journals.mcmaster.ca/mujph/article/download/4124/2729/18918).

**Mae La proxies:** No PPH figures were located. The WHO Safe Motherhood Needs Assessment at SMRU Mae La (2007–08) documented **active management of third stage of labor as standard observed practice**, no drug stock-outs, and correct partogram use >90% — the bundle most strongly associated with PPH prevention (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25652646/). The absence of hemorrhage as a flagged mortality driver in UNHCR site reports (1 maternal death in 2017, 0 in 2018) is consistent with, but cannot prove, low PPH mortality.

### 2.4 Neonatal mortality within 28 days

**Mae La** has the stronger data: UNHCR HIS reported **NNMR = 8 per 1,000 live births (2017)**, meeting the <20 standard (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/39ea9ee8-f0f1-3911-a9c5-b75ce55bc944/Thailand_2017_Maela.pdf). This continues a documented decline of 51% — from 21.8 (2008/09) to 10.7 (2011) per 1,000 — after introduction of a special care baby unit staffed by trained refugee medics (p=0.04) (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0072721); earlier SMRU statistics show 26/1,000 (2007–08) falling to 12/1,000 (2009–10) (https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/report/93713/thailand-neonatal-care-refugees-refugees). Early neonatal mortality among SMRU facility deliveries was 6.6/1,000 (95% CI 5.40–8.06, 2008–2015), comparable to Thailand's national rate (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322283421_Early_neonatal_mortality_and_neurological_outcomes_of_neonatal_resuscitation_in_a_resource-limited_setting_on_the_Thailand-Myanmar_border_A_descriptive_study).

**Cox's Bazar** lacks a published NNMR in the gathered evidence. Perinatal death surveillance (stillbirths + early neonatal deaths) only began in August 2023: **304 perinatal deaths Aug–Dec 2023** (78% in facilities/during referral) and **491 in 2024** (~10/week), linked to birth asphyxia, preterm birth, and growth restriction (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2024-09/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202023%20Final.docx.pdf; https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2025-08/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202024%20Final.docx.pdf).

**Derived estimate (explicit assumptions):** Using UNICEF's ">60 births/day in the camps" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12613593/), Aug–Dec 2023 ≈ 153 days ≈ 9,180 births. Then 304/9,180 ≈ **33 perinatal deaths per 1,000 total births** (includes stillbirths; the early-neonatal subset is not separable from the retrieved text). # Medical-Grade Refrigeration Procurement Analysis — 8-Site Rural MT/WY Hospital Network

**Prepared for:** Procurement Manager, 200-bed hospital network (rural Montana & Wyoming)
**Products evaluated:** Helmer Scientific GX Solutions (iPR125-GX, 25.2 cu ft, as representative), Thermo Fisher TSX Series (TSX2305PA 23 cu ft / TSX3005PA 29.2 cu ft), Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA (25.7 cu ft)

---

## 1. Bottom Line Up Front

**Recommended primary unit: Helmer Scientific GX Solutions (iPR125-GX or iPR105-GX undercounter for small clinics).** It is ETL-certified to NSF/ANSI 456 (CDC's preferred tier), posts the best documented chamber stability (0.06–0.75°C across models), and — critically for your 6–12 hour outages — has the longest documented controller battery in this comparison (20 hours), keeping alarms, display, and data logging alive through the entire outage event even though **none of the three units runs its compressor on battery**.

**Thermo TSX is a close, cheaper second** with a 120-month compressor warranty and the fastest documented door-opening recovery (2–3 min), but its alarm-battery backup duration is not published.

**Do not buy the Panasonic MDF-DU702VH-PA for this application.** It is a **-86°C ultra-low temperature (ULT) freezer**, not a vaccine refrigerator. It only fits the ultra-cold niche (CDC ultra-cold range: -90°C to -60°C, e.g., original Pfizer COVID-19 formulation). For routine refrigerated vaccines (2–8°C) it is the wrong product category, is not NSF/ANSI 456 certified, costs ~3x more, and consumes ~2x the electricity.

**Fleet-level planning numbers (8 sites, 10 years):** roughly **$225,000–$230,000** for Helmer or TSX refrigerators including monitoring and estimated PM contracts, versus **~$470,000** for the Panasonic ULT — and the ULT still leaves your refrigerated-vaccine requirement unsolved.

---

## 2. Critical Category Caveat

The CDC Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit (July 2026) defines required ranges (https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/hcp/downloads/storage-handling-toolkit.pdf):
- Refrigerators: **2°C to 8°C**
- Freezers: **-50°C to -15°C**
- Ultra-cold freezers: **-90°C to -60°C**

The Panasonic MDF-DU702VH-PA has a control range of **-40°C to -86°C** (https://www.phchd.com/global/-/media/biomedical/global/catalogues/MDF-ULT/MDF_DU702VH_DataSheet_E_0414.pdf). It cannot hold 2–8°C at all. It is appropriate only if one or more sites must stock ultra-cold products. This analysis evaluates it as specified, but flags that a like-for-like comparison would substitute a PHCbi pharmacy refrigerator (e.g., MPR series), which was not scoped.

---

## 3. Head-to-Head Specifications

| Criterion | Helmer iPR125-GX | Thermo TSX2305PA/3005PA | Panasonic MDF-DU702VH-PA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Category | Pharmacy/vaccine refrigerator | Pharmacy refrigerator | ULT freezer (-86°C) |
| Capacity | 25.2 cu ft / 714 L | 23 / 29.2 cu ft | 25.7 cu ft / 729 L |
| Temp range | +2°C to +10°C (setpoint 5°C) | 3–7°C (setpoint 5°C) | -40°C to -86°C |
| NSF/ANSI 456 | **Yes (ETL)** | **Yes** | No (ISO 13485, ENERGY STAR) |
| Controller battery | **20 hr (display & alarm)**, 12V lead-acid | Alarm battery (duration unpublished); chart recorder ~24 hr on 9V | Battery for controller/alarms (duration unpublished) |
| Compressor backup | None (generator required) | None (generator required) | None; **optional liquid CO2 backup kit (MDF-UB7-PW)** |
| Compressor | Variable-speed (VCC), R600a | V-drive variable-speed, R290 | 2× 750W variable-speed cascade, R-290/R-170 |
| Uniformity | ±1.0°C | 0.8–0.9°C (unloaded map) | Not published for chamber |
| Stability | **0.06–0.75°C** | 2.3°C | Not published |
| Energy | ~3.5 kWh/day (est.; class data below) | 3.2–4.0 kWh/day (documented) | 7.87–9.00 kWh/day (documented) |
| Warranty | 7 yr compressor / 2 yr parts / 1–2 yr labor | **120-month compressor** | 5 yr parts & labor |
| Documented price | $12,128.73 | $9,649–$14,620 (street–list) | $32,463.41 (list) |

Sources: Helmer TDS https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR125GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380420-1.pdf and https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR113GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380443-1.pdf; Helmer GX brochure https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2020-08/Refrigerator-GX-380410-1.pdf; TSX data sheets https://www.scientificlabs.com/handlers/libraryFiles.ashx?filename=Technical_Data_Sheets_T_TSX3005PV.pdf and ...T_TSX1205PV.pdf; TSX brochure https://documents.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LPD/brochures/COL114620%20Brochure%20refresh%20TSX%20FINAL%20FLR_BT.pdf; TSX user manual https://assets.thermofisher.com/TFS-Assets/LED/manuals/TSX%20Laboratory%20Refrigerator%20User%20Manual%20327929H01_RevG_English.pdf; Panasonic datasheet and product pages https://www.phchd.com/us/biomedical/preservation/ultra-low-freezers/mdf-du702vhpa; https://markitbiomedical.com/knowledge-center/files/11559_3_PHCBI_MDF_DU702VH_technical_spec_vf.pdf; https://daiscientific.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/PHCBI_MDF_DU702VH_product_sheet_vf-1.pdf; pricing: https://www.cmecorp.com/helmer-scientific-5115125-1-ipr125-gx-i-series-pharmacy-refrigerator-25-2-cu-ft-714-liters.html; https://www.terrauniversal.com/tsx-series-high-performance-pharmacy-refrigerators-thermo-fisher-scientific.html; https://www.capitolscientific.com/Thermo-Scientific-TSX2305PA-TSX-Series-High-Performance-Pharmacy-Refrigerator-Capacity-651L-115V; https://www.fishersci.com/shop/products/tsx-series-high-performance-pharmacy-refrigerators/TSX2305PA; https://www.thomassci.com/p/phcbi-vip-eco-energy-efficient-86c-ultra-low-temperature-upright-freezers

---

## 4. Battery Backup During 6–12 Hour Outages

**The single most important finding: none of these units' batteries power cooling.** All three stop refrigerating at the moment of grid loss unless fed by a generator or external battery system. The batteries only keep electronics alive. Your outage strategy must therefore be layered: unit battery (alarm/data continuity) + facility generator or thermal buffering (CDC water-bottle guidance) + DDL excursion SOP + backup-facility transport plan.

- **Helmer GX: 20 hours** of display-and-alarm backup on a rechargeable 12V lead-acid battery (TDS, GX brochure). This comfortably spans a 6–12 hour outage — staff retain local temperature display, alarms, min/max, and event logging for the entire event, and the unit's remote contacts stay live for monitoring systems on generator power. This is the strongest documented showing of the three.
- **Thermo TSX:** "Continuous charge provides full alarm function in case of power failure" (brochure); the optional chart recorder runs ~24 hours on a 9V battery; the 12V alarm battery must be replaced **at most every 12 months** (part 322533H01) per the user manual. A specific alarm-battery runtime in hours is **not published** — a gap to close with Thermo before purchase.
- **Panasonic:** battery supports the controller/alarms (service manual shows battery switch/PCB); runtime not published. Its unique feature is the **optional MDF-UB7-PW liquid CO2 backup**, which genuinely maintains cooling during power failure — but only for the ULT use case, and bulk CO2 delivery logistics across rural MT/WY would be a recurring operational burden.

**Corroborating outage context (your geography):** EIA Form 861 2023 data shows Montana statewide SAIDI of 118.7 min/yr (SAIFI 1.10) and Wyoming 156.2 min/yr (SAIFI 1.18) — but rural cooperatives are far worse: Fergus Electric (MT) 390.5 min, Lower Yellowstone 260.2 min, Powder River (WY) 205.5 min, High Plains (WY) 325.6 min (https://plainutility.com/state/mt; https://plainutility.com/state/wy). The national cooperative mean SAIDI is 476.3 min (https://plainutility.com/statistics). Major-event tail risk is real: Rocky Mountain Power's Wyoming 2025 report logs two loss-of-supply events of ~34–36 SAIDI-minutes each, and the November 13, 2025 WECC voltage-collapse disturbance interrupted ~54,000 customers (https://www.rockymountainpower.net/content/dam/pcorp/documents/en/rockymountainpower/rates-regulation/wyoming/filings/docket-20000-712-ea-26/RMP_Exhibit_1.1_Reliability_Report.pdf). Your 6–12 hour planning assumption is consistent with major-event behavior, not average days.

---

## 5. Temperature Recovery After Power Restoration

No vendor publishes a "post-6-hour-outage recovery" figure, so the documented proxies are door-opening recovery and pull-down time (unloaded chambers):

| Metric | Helmer | TSX | Panasonic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Door-opening recovery | To 8°C after 3-min opening: **9 min** (iPR125-GX); 10 min (iPR256-GX); 12 min (iLR113GX) | To 5°C after 1-min opening: **2 min** (TSX3005PV); 3 min (TSX1205PV) | Recovery after 60-sec door opening shown graphically; fast due to 80mm VIP insulation |
| Pull-down to setpoint | 37 min (largest iPR458-GX, 58.5 cu ft) | **9–10 min** (12–30 cu ft) | Multi-hour to -80°C (graph; exact figure not captured) |
| Chamber stability | **0.06–0.75°C** | 2.3°C | Not published |

Sources: Helmer TDS files (above); TSX data sheets (above); Panasonic datasheet (above).

**Interpretation for your scenario:** with doors kept closed during an outage, a loaded refrigerator buffered with water bottles (CDC-recommended specifically to "guard against temperature fluctuation... caused by a power failure") will typically still be within or near 2–8°C at restoration for a large share of 6–12 hour events; recovery to setpoint then behaves like pull-down — minutes for TSX and Helmer refrigerators. CDC guidance is to allow **2–7 days of stabilization (2–3 days for freezers) with min/max recording before returning vaccines** after installation or repair — apply the same discipline after any extended outage (https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/hcp/storage-handling/equipment.html). The Panasonic's VIP-plus insulation gives it the slowest warm-up during an outage, but that advantage is irrelevant if you don't need -80°C storage.

---

## 6. CDC Toolkit Compliance

| Requirement (CDC Toolkit) | Helmer GX | Thermo TSX | Panasonic ULT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1: NSF/ANSI 456-conforming unit preferred | **Yes — ETL certified** (https://www.helmerinc.com/nsf-ansi-456-certified) | **Yes — certified** (https://www.thermofisher.com/order/catalog/product/TSX3005PV) | No |
| Purpose-built, microprocessor + digital sensor (RTD), fan-forced circulation | Yes | Yes | Yes (but wrong temp class) |
| Continuous DDL ±0.5°C, ≥30-min logging, buffered probe, alarm, min/max | i.C3 supports monitoring; **a separate/companion DDL is still required** | Same — controller is not a substitute for the CDC-specified DDL | Same |
| Backup DDL for emergency transport | Required regardless of unit | Required | Required |
| Emergency SOP: monitor/pack/transport during outages | Facility responsibility | Facility responsibility | Facility responsibility |

Both Helmer and TSX satisfy the toolkit's **preferred** equipment tier. NSF/ANSI 456 (developed with CDC on the joint committee) certifies that units maintain 5°C ±3°C **across all storage locations under varying load and use** (https://www.helmerinc.com/nsf-ansi-456-certified) — meaningful for you because single-probe monitoring can miss out-of-range hot/cold spots in non-certified cabinets (https://blog.helmerinc.com/temperature-uniformity-for-vaccine-storage). The Panasonic is a Class IIa medical device with ISO 13485 certification but is **not** NSF/ANSI 456 tested; the CDC toolkit treats ultra-cold units as a special case, so it is compliant only for ultra-cold inventory.

**Action item either way:** budget a CDC-compliant DDL (±0.5°C, glycol-buffered probe, 30-min logging) per unit **plus** one backup DDL per site for transport, since built-in controllers do not satisfy the VFC DDL requirement on their own.

---

## 7. Remote Monitoring Over Spotty Cellular

**Native connectivity:**
- **Helmer i.Series:** RJ45 Ethernet with a documented RESTful API and Modbus TCP, exposing temperature, alarms, door status, and refrigeration-system data to third-party continuous-monitoring or BAS platforms (https://www.helmerinc.com/connectivity). No native cellular.
- **Thermo TSX:** "DeviceLink™ Connect ready" and compatible with Smart-Vue™ Pro wireless monitoring; dry remote-alarm contacts standard (https://www.thermofisher.com/order/catalog/product/TSX5005PA). No native cellular on TSX pharmacy models.
- **Panasonic:** visual/buzzer/remote (V-B-R) alarm contacts and optional chart recorder; no network stack on this model.

**For spotty-connectivity sites**, the documented best practice is a cellular DDL/gateway with **large local buffering and store-and-forward**. The SensoScientific SensoTag Cellular logger (4G, ±0.5°C, GPS, CDC/VFC-compliant, **100,000-reading on-device buffer** with unlimited cloud storage) is one documented option (https://www.sensoscientific.com/en-us/products/digital-temperature-sensor-sensotag-cellular/); its Wi-Fi OTA line is the alternative where broadband exists (https://www.sensoscientific.com/applications/remote-temperature-monitoring/). ## Answer: Red Rooster's "$5 Lunch" — the $5 quarter chicken & chips deal, available 11am–4pm daily

**The chain checks out as Red Rooster.** It was founded in 1972 in Kelmscott, a suburb of Perth, Western Australia, by brothers **Peter and Theo Kailis**, sons of Greek migrant George Kailis (the Kailis family, better known for its WA fishing, pearling and seafood businesses — George opened a Perth fish shop in 1926). Peter Kailis and nine partners bought an existing chicken shop in Kelmscott to launch the brand, which grew to ~80 stores before being sold to Coles Myer in the early 1980s ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Rooster); [Australian Food Timeline](https://australianfoodtimeline.com.au/red-rooster-founded/); [PerthNow, 2018](https://www.perthnow.com.au/wa/hawaiian-pack-inventor-peter-kailis-still-enjoys-a-red-rooster-favourite-ng-b88738741z); [Realcommercial, 2025](https://www.realcommercial.com.au/news/poultry-pioneers-how-red-rooster-became-australias-answer-to-kfc)). It remains Australia's largest home-grown roast chicken chain, with the red branding ([Comcater](https://www.comcater.com.au/insights/customer-story/red-rooster/)).

**The promotion, as it stood in 2015, was called the "$5 Lunch."** Red Rooster's own marketing copy from July 2015 reads: *"Let us introduce you to your $5 lunch. We are serving up a quarter roast chicken and a small serve of our famous chips for only $5 (2650kJ). Available from 11am to 4pm daily"* ([OzBargain, 9 July 2015](https://www.ozbargain.com.au/node/202131)). That matches your recollection exactly: a portion of chicken, chips, a few bucks, cut off mid-afternoon.

**The "going since the 90s" part:** the format is much older than the $5 price. # "Nature's Castles: The Treehouse Reimagined" — Designers and Contemporaneous Sources

## Short answer

There was no single architectural firm. The three treehouses were created by **two specialist treehouse design/build firms working with a Philadelphia architecture firm of record**:

| Treehouse | Location | Designer/Builder |
|---|---|---|
| **Canopy Cathedral** | Near the Italian Water Garden / Large Lake | **Peter Nelson (with Jake Jacob), TreeHouse Workshop, Inc., Seattle, WA** |
| **The Birdhouse** | Terrace Woodland, near the Peirce-du Pont House | **Peter Nelson, TreeHouse Workshop, Inc.** |
| **Lookout Loft** | Forest Walk, behind the Peirce House, overlooking the Meadow | **Forever Young Treehouses, Burlington, VT** (co-founded by Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy; lead builder Erych Stauffer) |

**Matthew Millan Architects** (today Millan Architects, Philadelphia) states on its project pages that it "worked with Longwood Gardens and the two premier treehouse companies in the U.S. to create these unique arboreal structures," designing each treehouse "to respond to their individual settings and offer different interpretive opportunities" (https://millanarchitects.com/portfolio/institutional/natures-castles-the-treehouses-at-longwood-gardens-the-lookout-loft/). Longwood's own website independently confirms the Canopy Cathedral attribution: "Designed by Peter Nelson of TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. in Seattle" (https://longwoodgardens.org/gardens/lakes-district/large-small-lake).

## Design concept and construction, per contemporaneous (2008) sources

**1. Daily Local News (West Chester, PA), April 24, 2008** — "Longwood builds 'nature's castles' in the gardens' trees" (https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/). Written from the press preview (with third-graders from Pocopson Elementary as test climbers), it attributes the Canopy Cathedral to "Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob of Treehouse Workshop Inc in Seattle, Wash." — a two-story house "inspired by a Norwegian Stave Church" with cedar shakes, an intricate glass facade, and hand-carved fantastical creatures (unfinished on opening day). Lookout Loft is described as a 720-sq-ft handicapped-accessible Adirondack-style structure by Forever Young Treehouses with two joined viewing platforms held up by salvaged steel, "pie wood" handrails using matched natural contours, a citrus-oil-and-beeswax finish, and a "pin foundation [with] concrete footings with extended steel rods that go between the tree roots and cause no damage." The Birdhouse (reported here at 320 sq ft, ~20 ft up) was built from salvaged dairy-barn wood over a preserved rotted trunk with a viewing window. Director Paul Redman is quoted on the celebratory-trees concept.

**2. The Reporter (Lansdale, PA), April 24, 2008**, Brian Bingaman — "The sky's the limit at treehouse exhibit" (https://www.thereporteronline.com/2008/04/24/the-skys-the-limit-at-treehouse-exhibit/). The richest construction detail: the project was "two years in the making"; all three houses sit on "pin foundations" of sets of five-foot steel pipes rather than being bolted to trees or poured on concrete, so root systems are undisturbed. It documents the salvaged-materials palette — beams from a dismantled toothpaste factory in Toronto (the "random holes" are telltale clues), an old dairy barn in Chimacum, WA; storm/landslide-damaged Douglas firs; wildfire-salvaged Oregon logs; Vermont cedar, "ironwood" and eastern hemlock; sustainably harvested Brazilian hardwood. It credits the Canopy Cathedral's prow window to Scheel & Sharp of Norristown and quotes Forever Young's Bill Allen: "These trees have been waiting for a treehouse for 100 years." It also notes a documentary on the build aired on NBC-10 on April 28, 2008.

**3. Delaware County Daily Times, April 24, 2008**, Bette Alburger — "Treehouses are looking up at Longwood Gardens" (https://www.delcotimes.com/2008/04/24/treehouses-are-looking-up-at-longwood-gardens/). Confirms all three attributions, notes Nelson is "author of the leading books on treehouses," details the Birdhouse's provenance (dairy farm in Washington State; floorboards from the Toronto toothpaste factory; rafters from a dismantled Vancouver warehouse; tight-grained Douglas fir from storm-felled trees), and quotes horticulture head Sharon Loving on the environmental brief: recycled/reclaimed lumber, no disturbed root systems, and houses that "do not rely on the trees for structural support."

**4. Philadelphia Inquirer, May 16, 2008**, Virginia A. Smith — "Lofty ideas" (https://www.inquirer.com/philly/entertainment/20080516_Lofty_ideas.html) and the companion profile "Builder makes trees accessible for all" (https://www.inquirer.com/philly/columnists/virginia_smith/20080516_Builder_makes_trees_accessible_for_all.html). Places the exhibit in the regional treehouse-exhibit wave (Longwood, Morris Arboretum, Tyler Arboretum), reports the ~$1 million cost and Nov. 23, 2008 run, and profiles Forever Young's universal-access mission.

**5. Lancaster Online, April 24, 2008**, Jane Holahan — "Treehouses get the Longwood Gardens treatment" (https://lancasteronline.com/features/entertainment/treehouses-get-the-longwood-gardens-treatment/article_b9546a06-8269-50ca-bb93-dbd4c0feb118.html). Per the search extract: the Canopy Cathedral's steel frame comprises 37 columns, 34 beams and 8 braces; Lookout Loft has 75+ feet of ramps to three platforms up to 14 feet high; and "the three treehouses were built as permanent structures" despite the exhibit being billed through Nov. 23. (Direct fetch was blocked, so I could only verify this via the search extract — treat exact figures as slightly less certain than in the fully fetched articles.)

## Quantitative summary and discrepancies

- **Canopy Cathedral:** 400 sq ft (Daily Local, Delco Times, Longwood's website) vs. 589 sq ft main floor + 118 sq ft balcony (The Reporter, Delaware Today). The 589/118 figures likely refer to the two floors individually; the discrepancy is unresolved.
- **Birdhouse:** 255 sq ft (The Reporter) vs. 320 sq ft (Daily Local, Delco Times) — possibly overall footprint vs. interior floor area.
- **Lookout Loft:** 720 sq ft (Daily Local, Delco Times) vs. 900 sq ft (The Reporter, Delaware Today).
- **Lookout Loft steel:** "13,000 pounds of salvaged steel" (Daily Local) vs. "more than 1,300 pounds" (Delco Times) — almost certainly a typo in one account; the true figure is unverified.
- **Timeline:** press preview ~April 23, 2008; public opening Arbor Day weekend (April 25–26, 2008); scheduled run through Nov. 23, 2008, but built as permanent pin-founded structures — all three remain at Longwood today.

**Bottom line:** if you need one name, the most consistently credited designer across 2008 sources and Longwood's own materials is **Peter Nelson of TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. (Seattle)**, who designed two of the three treehouses (Canopy Cathedral and the Birdhouse); **Forever Young Treehouses (Burlington, VT)** created the accessible Lookout Loft; and **Matthew Millan Architects (Philadelphia)** served as the collaborating architect of record on the ensemble. The April 24, 2008 Daily Local News and Reporter articles are the best contemporaneous sources describing both the design concept (Norwegian stave-church inspiration, Adirondack rusticism, universal accessibility, interpretive wood species) and the construction process (pin foundations, salvaged/reclaimed materials, two-year build).

# Progressive Disclosure vs. Persistent Navigation in ERP Interfaces for Manufacturing Supervisors Transitioning from AS/400: A Synthesis of Evidence

## 1. Executive Summary

**Direct head-to-head evidence comparing progressive disclosure against persistent navigation inside ERP systems — for 45–60-year-old production supervisors specifically — does not exist in the published literature I could locate.** The strongest available evidence comes from four adjacent literatures: web navigation usability studies, layered-interface experiments with older adults, ERP training/change-management research, and vendor-documented implementations. Synthesized, the evidence supports a **hybrid**: keep primary navigation **persistent and visible** (never hidden behind menus), scope the default view **by role**, and use **progressive disclosure for depth** (advanced and occasional functions), while keeping the core layout stable across simple and advanced modes.

Key quantitative anchors:

- Hiding navigation cuts discoverability "almost in half" and makes users **39% slower on desktop** (15% slower on mobile) (NN/g, 2016; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/hamburger-menus/; https://smartinsights.com/digital-marketing-strategy/are-hamburger-menus-hidden-navigation-good-for-ux/).
- Reduced-functionality "layered" interfaces measurably improve initial learning **for older adults most**, but transitioning between layers temporarily degrades performance on already-learned tasks (Leung et al., 2010, ACM TACCESS; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1838562.1838563).
- A meta-analysis of 60 samples (N=10,003) found older trainees take **δ = 1.25 SD longer** in training and perform **δ = −1.08 SD worse** than younger trainees — large effects that should directly inflate your time-to-competency budgets (https://repository.rice.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/a52e92f5-9aad-4df2-b9a3-2408db1108ff/content).
- Documented adaptive/role-based Fiori implementations report production-order confirmation time **−31%**, material-movement posting errors **−47%**, cognitive load **−34%**, SUS **58→78** (SSRN preprint; https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7488856), while a comprehensive-dashboard redesign at Oracle NetSuite began from **~80% user dissatisfaction** (https://rebeccamoores.myportfolio.com/netsuite).

---

## 2. Evidence Base and Its Limits

Before the synthesis, three honesty notes that should shape how much weight you place on each finding:

1. **Vendor numbers are mostly self-reported.** Forrester TEI studies are Microsoft-commissioned; SAP-partner case-study percentages (35–68% improvements) rarely describe controls or sample sizes. Treat directionally, not as point estimates.
2. **The controlled experiments are not ERP studies.** NN/g's navigation studies used websites; Leung et al. used a smartphone address book; the layered-interface learnability study (Forsey et al., 2024) used military HMI (https://oro.open.ac.uk/99849/). Transfer to green-screen-veteran supervisors is plausible but unproven.
3. **One well-designed study found no navigation-model effect at all.** A 44-participant experiment comparing linear, persistent, and semi-persistent menu structures found **no significant differences** in task success, completion time, satisfaction, or perceived usability (https://exa.ai/library/publication/g3ywsxwsrj5). The navigation debate is therefore really about *hiding vs. showing* and *context preservation under complexity*, not about which visible arrangement is optimal.

---

## 3. Progressive Disclosure vs. Persistent Navigation: What the Evidence Shows

### 3.1 Hiding primary navigation is reliably harmful

NN/g's quantitative study (179 participants, 6 sites, desktop + mobile, remote unmoderated testing) measured navigation use, time-to-navigation, task difficulty, content discoverability, and task time (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/hamburger-menus/; methodology: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/hidden-navigation-methodology/):

- Discoverability of content requiring navigation dropped ~**20%** under hidden navigation vs. visible/combo (Smart Insights summary of the same study).
- Desktop tasks were **39% slower** with hidden navigation; mobile **15% slower**. The desktop penalty — the environment where ERP supervisors work — was the largest.
- On one site with a corner-positioned hidden menu, only **17%** of users used it vs. a **42%** desktop average, and it took **33s vs. 25s** to find (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/find-navigation-desktop-not-hamburger/).
- Hidden navigation mostly harms content not reachable via in-page links — exactly the situation of ERP "advanced functions" buried under a generic menu.

The mechanism NN/g identifies is **recognition vs. recall**: persistent navigation continuously advertises what the system can do; hidden navigation forces users to remember it. For your cohort — whose entire recognition vocabulary is AS/400 menu structures (often literal, numbered, always-visible menus) — hiding navigation removes the one interaction pattern they already trust.

### 3.2 Progressive disclosure helps learning — with a documented transition cost

Nielsen's foundational treatment (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/progressive-disclosure/) claims improvements in **3 of usability's 5 components: learnability, efficiency of use, and error rate** — but with a critical caveat: *"You must get the right split between initial and secondary features."* Frequently needed functions must be disclosed up front; the initial display can't be overcrowded. Nielsen recommends deciding the split via **feature-usage instrumentation**, not intuition.

The controlled evidence for your demographic is Leung et al. (2010, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1838562.1838563; PDF: https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/edapt/papers/leung2010.pdf): 16 older adults (65–81) and 16 younger (21–36) learned tasks on either a 2-layer reduced-functionality interface or a full-functionality control:

- The reduced-functionality layer **better helped users master basic tasks and retain that ability 30 minutes later**.
- **Older participants benefited more than younger** — in initial-learning task time, perceived complexity, and preference.
- **The transition cost:** when users moved from the reduced to the full layer, *"performance on the previously learned tasks was negatively affected, but no negative impact was found on learning new, advanced tasks."*

Design implication: progressive disclosure works when the *core task layout stays identical* between simple and advanced modes, and only additional capability is revealed. A related study of layered device interfaces with four age groups (30–70) also raises the risk that layering introduces **mode errors** and slower operation when the same controls behave differently per layer (https://exa.ai/library/publication/3rdg0wt6l3v) — a strong argument against "simple mode / expert mode" toggles that reshuffle controls.

Forsey et al. (2024) extend this in a military-systems context: a progressive-disclosure-through-layered-interfaces pattern improved learnability (time-to-learn), but participant differences suggested **a customized approach is needed** rather than one uniform layering (https://oro.open.ac.uk/99849/; https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/10648046241273291).

### 3.3 Persistent context matters more as task complexity rises

A study comparing expandable (persistent-context) vs. sequential (partial-context) menus found expandable menus produced **more efficient performance and less disorientation specifically for highly complex retrieval tasks** (high path length, low path relevance) (https://benthamopen.com/contents/pdf/TOERGJ/TOERGJ-2-64.pdf). Inventory investigations and work-order troubleshooting on the floor are precisely "high path length, low path relevance" tasks — supervisors don't always know where the answer lives. Combined with §3.1, the pattern is: **persistent, visible structure for navigation; progressive disclosure only for depth.**

### 3.4 The older-worker baseline you must design around

- MIS Quarterly (2022, https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/46/1/1/1921/Helping-Older-Workers-Realize-Their-Full): older users' lower IT-task performance is driven by **declining information-processing speed**; **IT experience and IT self-efficacy buffer it; IT overload and effort cost aggravate it**. This is the single most design-relevant finding: every extra click, hidden option, and dense dashboard disproportionately penalizes your cohort.
- The training meta-analysis (Rice University, https://repository.rice.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/a52e92f5-9aad-4df2-b9a3-2408db1108ff/content): older trainees perform worse (ρ = −0.14, k=34, N=5,642; δ = −1.08, k=21, N=1,242), take more time (ρ = 0.19, k=15, N=2,780; **δ = 1.25**, k=12, N=664), and have lower post-training self-efficacy (ρ = −0.08). δ = 1.25 on training time is a *large* effect — roughly the 89th percentile of the younger-trainee time distribution. Crucially, **no support was found for pacing or instructional approach as moderators** — meaning interface design and elapsed practice time, not training format gimmicks, carry the burden.
- A skill-acquisition study with 52 adults aged 50–80 over 4 consecutive days found **age and fluid intelligence predicted initial performance and improvement rate**, while crystallized intelligence predicted speed on familiar task types (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2585421/). Your AS/400 veterans have high crystallized domain knowledge (BOMs, routings, lot control) — the interface should anchor new learning in that vocabulary.
- Individualized, client-centered training produced significant difficulty reductions for workers 50–75 (computers and phones p<0.01; internet/email p=0.02–0.04) (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/b5b9/e9a85eb7f9ca550a6b1044bb68d5ba431ab6.pdf), and a multi-component programme for employees 50+ (n=633, mean age 55) improved self-efficacy and stress coping with 6-month persistence (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10433-022-00715-0).
- The Urban Institute's recommendations for older-worker digital training: **build confidence, leverage peer learning, assess digital fluency, teach skills in context** (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/104771/digital-skills-and-older-workers.pdf).

## 4. Documented Implementations: SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365

### 4.1 SAP S/4HANA (Fiori) — the role-based reference case

- **Supervisor persona design.** SAP's "Manage Process Orders" Fiori app is explicitly designed "keeping the supervisor persona in mind": an **analytical list page** (worklist table of process orders with status, quantity, progress) with drill-down to a details page showing master and transaction data "all in one place" — designed to eliminate switching between apps and manual transactions (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/one-stop-view-for-production-supervisor-manage-process-order/ba-p/13507308). This is the canonical progressive-disclosure *done right* pattern: one persistent worklist, depth on demand.
- **Fiori's first design principle is role-based visibility** — apps and data scoped to the user's role (https://ijrmeet.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/MS_240304_Enhancing-User-Experience-with-SAP-Fiori-Design-Systems-478-485.pdf; https://www.drhu.eu/reports/2017-RuudZandbergen-DesigningWithFIORI.pdf).
- **Fiori vs. classic SAP GUI:** a 12-participant lab study with Tobii eye-tracking on materials-management and HCM cases found the simplified UI improved segment durations, heat maps, and perceived usability versus the transactional GUI (https://theses.cz/id/7tnw07/zaverecna_prace.pdf).
- **Quantified outcomes (vendor/partner-reported, uncontrolled):**
  - Fiori reduces steps for common tasks by up to **55%** and total task time by over **50%** (NTT DATA; https://nttdata-solutions.com/us/blog/get-more-out-of-sap-s-4hana-with-sap-fiori/).
  - An implementation combining Fiori, Screen Personas, and RPA reported productivity **+35%**, process completion time **−42%**, error rates **−68%**; Screen Personas role-specific simplification reportedly cuts **training time up to 60%** while improving task completion (WJARR; https://wjarr.com/sites/default/files/fulltext_pdf/WJARR-2022-0212.pdf).
  - A partner pharma case: navigation time **−30%**, key-process time **−20%**, satisfaction **+25%** (https://itp.biz/sap-fiori-and-sap-s-4hana-better-user-experience/).
  - India Glycols (IBM case): order-to-pay report retrieval **−91%** (12 minutes → 60 seconds); **$200K** saved via Fiori apps/dashboards (https://www-api.ibm.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:4797d029-b161-4bca-a870-d3888f6ee3e7/original/as/63038563.pdf).
- **The most rigorous-adjacent SAP data point** (quasi-experimental, mixed-methods, but a recent SSRN preprint — treat with caution): an adaptive-Fiori framework across manufacturing and financial-services cases reported production-order confirmation time **−31%**, material-movement posting errors **−47%**, cognitive load **−34%**, and **SUS 58 → 78** (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7488856). ### 4.2 Oracle NetSuite — the cautionary tale about comprehensive dashboards, and the phased "staircase"

- **Comprehensive dashboards failed their users.** Oracle NetSuite's own dashboard redesign research found **~80% of customers dissatisfied** and unwilling to recommend the dashboard, citing "an unpredictable experience and an outdated, confusing UI" — with **8 different button types performing the same action, 3 tab types, 2 context menus** (https://rebeccamoores.myportfolio.com/netsuite). This is the clearest documented failure mode of the "everything on one screen" approach: inconsistency and unpredictability, not information volume alone, drove dissatisfaction.
- **Perceived difficulty is high, and effort-reduction messaging alone doesn't drive adoption.** A UTAUT study of 84 NetSuite users found **performance expectancy significantly affected intention, but effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions did not**; users rated NetSuite's difficulty "relatively high" yet continued using it because of management commitment (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/373950448_Evaluation_of_ERP_Oracle_NetSuite_Implementation_Using_the_Unified_Theory_of_Acceptance_and_Use_of_Technology_UTAUT_Model_to_Create_a_Sustainable_Business). - **Module go-live ≠ proficiency.** A pharmaceutical manufacturer 18 months post-go-live had work orders flowing in NetSuite while planning still ran on spreadsheets with a single planner hand-exploding 140+ multi-level BOMs — the interface was live, but deep-function competency lagged (https://saloraerp.com/case/case-study-netsuite-supply-chain-for-pharmaceuticals-manufacturer/). A 12-month pre/post study at a mid-sized fulfillment company also listed training requirements, legacy integration, and change resistance as the standing challenges (https://www.ijsrm.net/index.php/ijsrm/article/view/4551/3753).

### 4.3 Microsoft Dynamics 365 — work-order UX and measured interaction-cost reduction

- **Work order creation is guided by scenario, not exposed all at once.** Microsoft documents six creation methods (manual, from case, from agreement, from opportunity, Power Automate, Web API) selected via a scenario table — a progressive-disclosure structure where dispatchers see only the path relevant to their situation (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/field-service/create-work-order).
- **The 2023 wave-2 work-order experience redesign** simplified create/manage/schedule with "more information at a glance," header-plus-contextual-tabs forms, and — per Microsoft's 2024 announcement — **reduced clicks by up to 39%**, inline editing of commonly changed fields, and Copilot summaries to speed orientation (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/field-service/work-order-experience; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics-365/blog/it-professional/2024/03/25/introducing-the-new-work-order-experience-in-dynamics-365-field-service/).

Supply Chain Management TEI (5 organizations): production volume capacity from **10–15% faster time-to-market**, unplanned downtime **−2–3%**, revenue up to **+5%** (https://sunrise.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Dynamics365SupplyChainManagementTEI_FINAL.pdf; https://blog.cfbs-us.com/microsoft-dynamics/dynamics-365-supply-chain-management-cost-savings-and-business-benefits). The combined Finance+SCM TEI composite (7 customers, ~10,000-FTE manufacturer) models **6% shop-floor staffing reduction** and **20% finance productivity gain** from automation, better UX, and reduced rework (https://marketingassets.microsoft.com/gdc/gdcOpHDtz/original).
- **User-centered redesign evidence:** a Dynamics 365 Business Central case for a trading SME using contextual inquiry, journey mapping, and usability testing achieved a **100% task success rate, 40% reduction in task completion time, and high SUS scores** (https://exa.ai/library/publication/xg1yfls3khj).
